name: Malawi
summary_text: Malawi criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. Penal Code sections 153, 154 and 156 remain in force, and the provisions reach gender identity directly through their application to people whose gender expression departs from expectations; Human Rights Watch reports that people whose gender expression differs from expectations are the most likely to be targeted. Under sections 153 and 156 men face up to fourteen years' imprisonment and women five years, and the sections were before the courts in 2024 as carrying up to fourteen years.  On 28 June 2024 a three-member panel of the Constitutional Court rejected the challenge to those sections. The application had been brought by Dutch national Jan Willen Akster and Jana Gonani, a trans woman who received an eight-year sentence in a men's prison in December 2021. Faith-based groups filed briefs and religious leaders led nationwide protests claiming the case sought to legalise same-sex marriage. The court left any reform to parliament. Human Rights Watch called the decision a dark day and warned that it exposes LGBT people to heightened risks of arbitrary arrest and violence.  Enforcement has been intermittent and evasive rather than absent. A justice-ministerial moratorium on arrests announced in 2012 was reaffirmed in December 2015, then suspended by the Mzuzu High Court in 2016 following litigation by religious leaders, leaving its legality contested. In April 2018 police in Mzuzu arrested Limbani Sibande, 24, for suspected homosexuality and charged him under section 156 rather than section 153, a choice that circumvented the six-year moratorium while both laws faced constitutional challenge; police spokespersons confirmed the custody.  Arbitrary detention and ill-treatment by police are documented. A 61-page Human Rights Watch report released on 26 October 2018, based on interviews with 45 LGBT people in Lilongwe and Blantyre alongside lawyers, activists and officials, found that police arbitrarily arrested and detained transgender people and at times assaulted them. Two men arrested on 7 December 2015 suffered house ransacking and assault by neighbours, threats of being burned alive, attempted extortion, forced stripping, forced medical and HIV and sexually transmitted infection examinations, and distribution of photographs on social media by community police.  Care access is compromised on gender-expression grounds. The same 2018 report records a trans man beaten and then refused treatment, and nurses mocking people presenting for HIV tests. Detention itself carries risk: Malawi's prisons were described as harsh in a 2011 United States State Department human rights report, and that report documented the July 2011 protest killings in which 20 people died.  Marriage and legal recognition are closed. The Marriage, Divorce and Family Relations Law, in force from 17 April 2015, bans all same-sex marriages and unions, states that gender is assigned at birth, and does not permit a person who has undergone gender reassignment surgery to marry someone of that person's prior gender. No process for legal gender recognition is described in the sources. There are no broad legal protections against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity; since 2019 the only limited protection is against hate speech, through sections 22(1-d) and 30(2-d) of the Communications (Broadcasting) Regulations 2019, which bar broadcast content likely to incite hatred on account of gender identity or sexual preference.  Official hostility is documented at the highest levels. In April 2010 President Bingu wa Mutharika called same-sex marriage evil and bad before the eyes of God, and in July 2011 he threatened activists Undule Mwakasungula and Gift Trapence, saying he would hunt them in their homes and smoke them out, forcing them into hiding amid treason threats. In January 2016 People's Party spokesperson Ken Msonda posted that gay people are worse than dogs and should be killed; the Malawi Law Society filed charges but the director of public prosecution took over the matter and discontinued it on 21 January. The Muslim Association of Malawi called for the death penalty for gay people in February 2014, and on 4 January 2017 thousands across 28 districts marched against legalising homosexuality in protests led by the Episcopal Conference of Malawi and the Evangelical Association of Malawi. Peter Sawali was arrested in 2010 and given a 60-day sentence for posting Gay rights are human rights posters in Blantyre.

name: Mayotte
summary_text: Mayotte stands under the national framework of France. Identity-document rules, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute, the marriage regime and the rules governing places of deprivation of liberty apply on the island as French law, and the French prison framework binds Mayotte's establishments as French prisons.  Nothing in that framework criminalises trans people or being in a same-sex relationship. Same-sex marriage has been lawful on the island since the 1975 vote to remain within the Republic, and Mayotte is one of few jurisdictions in Africa and in the Muslim-majority world where such marriages can be performed.  Placement in custody follows the gender marker carried on the identity document rather than anatomy, under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code. Reporting of 12 January 2018 documents that trans women incarcerated in France are accordingly held in all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them, and the French prison framework extends to local jails as French establishments.  France's detention-places watchdog CGLPL concluded in an opinion of 25 May 2021 that there is a persistence of serious violations of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty. That assessment rests on referrals received since 2010 concerning some forty transgender people and on inspections that interviewed eight trans women and one trans man at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse; the establishments it covers include those on Mayotte.  The simplification of legal gender change voted by the French National Assembly is French law and therefore applies on Mayotte, giving trans residents access to the simplified civil-status procedure.  Formal entitlement and lived experience diverge on the island. A report of 23 May 2023 describes a teacher at the university centre of Mayotte and his Malagasy partner, pseudonym Abdallah, completing a long and complicated path before marrying at Sada Town Hall, in a predominantly Muslim society where the rights the law confers are not matched by social acceptance.

sources.documents: Foundation of legal status: decriminalisation of same-sex sexual activity in private, retained in 1810 Code and followed in French colonies; applies in Mayotte as French department.

sources.title: Vichy Article 334 / Article 331 - discriminatory age of consent law
sources.documents: Historical enforcement: raised age of consent to 21 for homosexual relations vs 15 for heterosexual (6 Aug 1942, moved 8 Feb 1945), lowered to 18 in 1974, repealed 4 Aug 1982 to equalise at 15.
sources.detail: No URL visible; citation details in text: dates 6 August 1942, 8 February 1945, 1974, 4 August 1982 under President Francois Mitterrand, opposition of Jean Foyer.
